clusters.name: Your stepfather Desmond joining the household, 1987
clusters.reason: Around 1987, when you began secondary school, three shifts fell together: your distance from Desmond, your pull toward your father, and your move onto the chess squad where you felt out of your depth. That autumn your stepmother left over the question of a baby, and the household was unsettled; your anxiety rose as you pushed yourself hard to qualify. These months held shifts in how you stood with the men in your life and a spike in your own anxiety, with no shifts in anyone else's showing then.

clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1992
clusters.reason: Your grandfather Gordon died in June 1991 after years of kidney disease. Around the same time and after, shifts piled up through your late teens: your move to the conservatory in September 1991 where you leaned hard on Rafe; a wrist injury that stopped your playing that October and sent your anxiety and functioning both down; a blow-up with Rafe in November; you getting high and absorbed in radios through late autumn; and by early 1992, you lost and low, unable to get going. Your mother filled in your college forms, leaving you underfunctioning. The autumn of 1989, the family moved into the rebuilt Hollin Road house, loud and cramped, and you liked late nights and dropped chess and debate. Your grandfather's death came at a hinge: you had no footing with him gone and your mother about to remarry.

clusters.name: Your failed audition for the national orchestra, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around 2001 and 2002, three major shifts came together for you: you ran out of steam for performing and your anxiety and functioning both fell; your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer and underwent operations and chemotherapy; and you had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town. By September 2002, you were on poor terms with family and friends, distant from your parents. You left Thornbury for Gull Harbour that autumn, met Marisol in early 2003, moved to Fenwick to live with her by June, and split from her by October. Once back in Thornbury that November, you sank into a deep depression, could not face your family, and relied on friends instead. Your parents seemed a world away. Your anxiety rose as you distanced from them. By January 2004 you began swimming and returned to your therapist, and your functioning started to come back. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home that autumn of 2003 and died in February 2004. The period holds your own burnout alongside your grandmother's illness and death, and the months when you cut yourself off from family.
